plan: Seven new SAT R&W items written with denser, more academic passages after batches 42-43 rated no item hard: controlled-variable inference (shade leaves), cross-text rejection with concession (author intention vs text), share-of-decline data claim (water use), colon before a complex list, evaluative transition (tellingly), function of a qualifying sentence, synthesis of a consequence (Tacoma Narrows). Difficulty provisional.

passages.title: Shade and sun
passages.text: In many plant species, individuals that grow in shade produce larger but thinner leaves than individuals of the same species grown in full sun. In a greenhouse study, seedlings of a forest herb raised in shade and then moved into full sun suffered more leaf damage than seedlings raised in full sun from the start, even though the two groups had the same total leaf area when the move occurred. These results suggest that ______

passages.title: Letters and meaning
passages.text:
Text 1
Some literary scholars hold that a novel's meaning is fixed by what its author intended. On this view, when readers disagree about a passage, an author's letters or notebooks should settle the dispute, since they offer direct evidence of intention.

Text 2
Other scholars argue that readers encounter only the published book and that interpretation must therefore rest on the text itself. These scholars do grant that an author's letters can be useful in one respect: they can show what a word meant to writers and readers at the time the book was written, a meaning that may since have changed.

passages.title: Where the water went
passages.text:
A city's total water use fell from 120 million to 96 million liters per day between 2010 and 2020. The table shows average daily use, in millions of liters, by category.
Lawn and garden watering: 40 in 2010, 22 in 2020
Indoor household use: 55 in 2010, 50 in 2020
Commercial and other use: 25 in 2010, 24 in 2020
A city analyst claims that most of the decline in total water use came from reduced lawn and garden watering.

passages.title: Three venues
passages.text: This year's festival used three ______ a converted grain mill, which hosted the film screenings; a riverside tent, which held the evening concerts; and the town library, which housed the poetry readings.

passages.title: Second thoughts
passages.text: When the photographer's first exhibition opened, many critics dismissed the prints as mere technical exercises, unworthy of comparison with painting. ______ several of those same critics praised her compositions a decade later, once photography had gained acceptance as an art, suggesting that their original objection had been to the medium rather than to her work.

passages.title: A dissenting reading
passages.text: For decades, historians described the town's 1890s building boom as the work of outside investors who arrived with the railroad. Historian Imani Torres questions this account. Examining property records, she found that more than half of the new buildings were financed by local families who had lived in the town since before the railroad came. Torres does not deny that the railroad mattered; rather, she argues that it gave existing residents a reason to invest in their own town.

passages.title: Notes on a bridge
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- The Tacoma Narrows Bridge in Washington State opened in July 1940.
- Its deck was unusually narrow and shallow for its length.
- In November 1940, a steady wind of about 40 miles per hour set the deck twisting.
- The twisting grew until the main span collapsed; no people were killed.
- Engineers afterward began testing bridge designs with scale models in wind tunnels.

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: seedlings grown in shade develop less total leaf area over their lifetimes than seedlings that are grown in full sun.
choices.B: thin leaves are generally better suited than thick leaves to the harsh conditions of growing in full sun.
choices.C: the leaves a plant produces early in its growth may limit how well it can tolerate a later change in light.
choices.D: the forest herb cannot grow successfully in full sun at any stage of its life, regardless of how it was raised.

candidates.evidence: even though the two groups had the same total leaf area
candidates.explanation: Because leaf area was equal, the extra damage must come from the kind of leaves the shade-raised seedlings had already grown. That suggests early leaf development limits a plant's response to later light.

A.rationale: The text says the two groups had the same total leaf area when they were moved.

B.rationale: The shade-raised seedlings, with thinner leaves, suffered more damage in full sun, which points the other way.

D.rationale: Seedlings raised in full sun from the start are not described as failing, so this overstates the finding.

hints: What differed between the two groups, and what was the same?

strategy.explanation: Identify the controlled variable, then ask what explains the difference.

candidates.remember: When a text rules out one explanation, the answer is usually the remaining one.

candidates.stem: Based on the texts, how would the scholars in Text 2 most likely respond to the view in Text 1?

choices.A: They would deny that letters settle disputes about meaning but allow letters to clarify what words meant in the past.
choices.B: They would agree that letters should settle disputes, provided the letters were written while the novel was being composed.
choices.C: They would reject any use at all of an author's letters, since such letters are never part of the published book.
choices.D: They would argue that notebooks are more reliable than letters as evidence of what an author intended to say.

candidates.evidence: These scholars do grant that an author's letters can be useful in one respect
candidates.explanation: Text 2 rejects Text 1's central claim (letters settle meaning) but concedes one use: clarifying historical word meanings.

B.rationale: Text 2 says interpretation must rest on the text itself, so it would not let letters settle disputes.

C.rationale: Text 2 explicitly grants that letters can help show what a word meant at the time.

D.rationale: Text 2 does not compare kinds of evidence of intention; it rejects intention as the basis for meaning.

hints: What does Text 2 reject, and what does it concede?

strategy.explanation: Separate the main disagreement from the concession.

candidates.remember: Cross-text answers often combine a disagreement with a partial concession.

candidates.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the analyst's claim?

choices.A: Lawn and garden watering fell by 45 percent from 2010 to 2020, the largest percent drop of any category.
choices.B: Indoor household use was the largest single category of the city's water use in both 2010 and in 2020.
choices.C: Total water use in the city fell by 24 million liters per day from 2010 to 2020.
choices.D: Lawn and garden watering fell by 18 million liters per day, or 18 of the 24 million-liter total decline.

candidates.evidence: most of the decline in total water use came from reduced lawn and garden watering
candidates.explanation: The claim is about share of the decline. Lawn watering fell by 18 of the 24 million liters, which is most of the decline; only choice D compares the two amounts.

A.rationale: A large percent drop in one category does not show what share of the total decline that category accounts for.

B.rationale: This describes the size of a category, not the source of the decline.

C.rationale: This states the size of the decline but does not show where it came from.

hints: What does "most of the decline" require you to compare?

strategy.explanation: Compute each category's change and compare it with the total change.

candidates.remember: A claim about share of a change needs the part compared with the whole.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: a converted grain mill, which hosted the film screenings
candidates.explanation: An independent clause ("This year's festival used three venues") introduces a list, so a colon is correct.

A.rationale: A semicolon must separate two independent clauses or items in a complex list; it cannot introduce the list.

C.rationale: Without punctuation, the list runs directly into the clause it explains.

D.rationale: "Which were" makes the rest of the sentence a long dependent clause, and the list's semicolons then separate fragments.

hints: Is the first part of the sentence a complete clause?

strategy.explanation: Check what comes before and after the blank.

candidates.remember: A colon follows a complete clause and introduces a list or explanation.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.evidence: suggesting that their original objection had been to the medium
candidates.explanation: The critics' change of mind reveals something about their earlier objection, so "Tellingly" marks the later praise as revealing.

A.rationale: The later praise contrasts with the early dismissal; it is not similar to it.

B.rationale: The critics' later praise was not caused by their earlier dismissal.

D.rationale: The second sentence adds new information rather than restating the first.

hints: What does the later praise reveal about the earlier dismissal?

strategy.explanation: Label the relationship before reading the choices.

candidates.remember: Use "tellingly" when a detail reveals something about what came before.

candidates.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the last sentence in the text?

choices.A: It presents evidence from property records that supports Torres's claim about local families.
choices.B: It explains why earlier historians believed that investors from outside the town caused the 1890s boom.
choices.C: It concedes that the earlier account was correct and that Torres has withdrawn her objection.
choices.D: It limits Torres's challenge to the earlier account by granting a factor that account stressed.

candidates.evidence: Torres does not deny that the railroad mattered
candidates.explanation: The last sentence limits Torres's challenge: she accepts the railroad's importance but reframes its role as motivating local investment.

A.rationale: The evidence from property records appears in the previous sentence.

B.rationale: The sentence describes Torres's view, not the reasoning of earlier historians.

C.rationale: Torres still argues that local families drove the boom; she only grants that the railroad mattered.

hints: Does the last sentence add evidence, explain others' views, or limit Torres's claim?

strategy.explanation: Describe what the sentence does in relation to the sentences before it.

candidates.remember: "Does not deny ... rather" signals a qualification.

candidates.stem: The student wants to explain how the collapse influenced later bridge design. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: The Tacoma Narrows Bridge opened in July 1940 and collapsed in November of the same year, although no people were killed.
choices.B: After the Tacoma Narrows Bridge twisted apart in a steady wind in 1940, engineers began testing designs on models in wind tunnels.
choices.C: The deck of the Tacoma Narrows Bridge, which opened in July 1940, was unusually narrow and shallow for the length of its main span.
choices.D: A steady wind of about 40 miles per hour set the deck of the Tacoma Narrows Bridge twisting until it fell.

candidates.evidence: Engineers afterward began testing bridge designs with scale models in wind tunnels.
candidates.explanation: The goal is the collapse's influence on later design. Only choice B links the collapse to the new practice of wind-tunnel testing.

A.rationale: This gives the dates and outcome of the collapse but not its influence on later design.

C.rationale: This describes the bridge's design, not how the collapse changed later designs.

D.rationale: This explains the collapse but not its influence on later bridge design.

hints: Which note describes what happened afterward?

strategy.explanation: Find the choice that connects the event to its later effect.

candidates.remember: Synthesis choices must address the stated goal.
